root.note: Latin parabola comes from Greek parabolḗ, ‘comparison’. The Late Latin verb parabolare, ‘to speak’, is the usual source of parlare.

history: Parlare does not come from the classical Latin verb for speaking, loqui. Its source is parabola, a Greek loan meaning ‘comparison’ and then ‘parable’, a story with a hidden message. Christian preachers used parabola a great deal, and in Late Latin the word moved from ‘parable’ to ‘speech’ and gave the verb parabolare. The syllables wore down: parabolare, paraulare, parlare. The same thing happened in French, where parler gave English parley, parlour and parliament. Italian parola, ‘word’, belongs to the same family, and so does the English word parable. When you learn Italian, parlare covers ‘speak’ and ‘talk’: parlo italiano, parliamo del contratto.
historyEinfach: Parlare comes from Late Latin parabolare. That comes from parabola, ‘comparison, story’. People used the word for ‘parable’, then for ‘speech’, and the verb became shorter over the centuries. English parliament, parley and parable are relatives.

elsewhere.text: Spanish uses hablar, from Latin fabulari, ‘to chat’, for the same idea. Portuguese falar has the same origin. So the Romance languages did not all choose the same verb to replace Latin loqui.
